meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · Biology · solo · run 3
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 6 of 24 credited claims; 3 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Matched Stiffler TEM-1 scores improve Firnberg fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: For mutations with a score in the matched Stiffler assay, a linear calibration from Stiffler to Firnberg scores achieved lower five-fold held-out MAE than the one-hot ridge comparator. Calibration was fitted only on the training fold; predictions fall back to ridge if no matched source score is available. The prediction test re-runs this transfer using the public matched assay data.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0045

claim.statement: Cross-assay calibrated Stiffler scores predict held-out Firnberg growth scores more accurately than one-hot ridge regression.

artifacts.title: Matched Firnberg TEM-1 scores improve Stiffler fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: For mutations with a score in the matched Firnberg assay, a linear calibration from Firnberg to Stiffler scores achieved lower five-fold held-out MAE than the one-hot ridge comparator. Calibration was fitted only on the training fold; predictions fall back to ridge if no matched source score is available. The prediction test re-runs this transfer using the public matched assay data.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0110

claim.statement: Cross-assay calibrated Firnberg scores predict held-out Stiffler growth scores more accurately than one-hot ridge regression.

artifacts.title: Position-dependent cross-assay transfer improves Firnberg TEM-1 prediction
artifacts.summary: A ridge model using the matched Stiffler score, mutation position, and their interaction reduced held-out Firnberg-score error. On two fresh 10-fold random-split repetitions, it outperformed one-hot ridge, including on the full held-out set by falling back to ridge for the rare mutation without a matched source score. The released predictor fits only on training-fold labels and uses the matched public Stiffler assay scores for transfer.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0045

claim.statement: For BLAT_ECOLX_Firnberg_2014, position-dependent calibrated transfer from Stiffler scores improves held-out prediction over the one-hot ridge comparator.

artifacts.title: Position-dependent cross-assay transfer improves Stiffler TEM-1 prediction
artifacts.summary: A ridge model using the matched Firnberg score, mutation position, and their interaction reduced held-out Stiffler-score error. On two fresh 10-fold random-split repetitions, it outperformed one-hot ridge, including on the full held-out set by falling back to ridge for mutations without a matched source score. The released predictor fits only on training-fold labels and uses the matched public Firnberg assay scores for transfer.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0110

claim.statement: For BLAT_ECOLX_Stiffler_2015, position-dependent calibrated transfer from Firnberg scores improves held-out prediction over the one-hot ridge comparator.

artifacts.title: Residue-aware cross-assay transfer improves Firnberg TEM-1 prediction
artifacts.summary: Using matched Stiffler measurements, mutation position, and wild-type/alternate amino-acid identity in a ridge transfer model improved held-out Firnberg prediction. Validation used two 10-fold random-split repetitions; the single mutation without a paired source score used the standard sequence-ridge fallback. The released code implements the same transfer and fallback for held-out inputs.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0045

claim.statement: Residue-aware transfer calibrated on matched Stiffler scores improves held-out BLAT_ECOLX_Firnberg_2014 prediction over one-hot ridge regression.

artifacts.title: Position-interaction transfer improves Stiffler TEM-1 prediction
artifacts.summary: A ridge model combining matched Firnberg assay scores with mutation position and score-by-position interactions improved held-out Stiffler prediction. Validation used two 10-fold random-split repetitions; mutations without a paired source score use the standard sequence-ridge fallback. The released code implements the same transfer and fallback for held-out inputs.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0110

claim.statement: Position-interaction transfer calibrated on matched Firnberg scores improves held-out BLAT_ECOLX_Stiffler_2015 prediction over one-hot ridge regression.

artifacts.title: Cross-assay transfer improves KCNE1 functional prediction
artifacts.summary: Using matched KCNE1 expression scores, mutation position, and amino-acid identity in a ridge transfer model improved held-out function prediction over one-hot ridge. Validation used two 10-fold random-split repetitions; unpaired variants fall back to sequence ridge.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0041

claim.statement: Position- and residue-aware transfer from KCNE1 expression scores improves held-out KCNE1 functional prediction.

artifacts.title: Cross-assay transfer improves KCNE1 expression prediction
artifacts.summary: Using matched KCNE1 function scores, mutation position, and amino-acid identity in a ridge transfer model improved held-out expression prediction over one-hot ridge. Validation used two 10-fold random-split repetitions; unpaired variants fall back to sequence ridge.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [-0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0044

claim.statement: Position- and residue-aware transfer from KCNE1 functional scores improves held-out KCNE1 expression prediction.

artifacts.title: Pooled substitution identity improves CASP3 activity prediction
artifacts.summary: Appending a one-hot wild-type-to-alternate amino-acid substitution encoding to the one-hot mutant sequence, then fitting ridge regression, improved CASP3 activity prediction over sequence-only ridge. Improvement was observed on fresh random splits and when entire residue positions were held out. The released script trains on the public training set and writes predictions for evaluator inputs.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0381, 95% CI [-0.0626, -0.0127], beyond the minimum effect 0.0092)

claim.statement: Sequence-plus-substitution-identity ridge improves held-out CASP3 activity prediction over sequence-only ridge, including in residue-position-grouped validation.

artifacts.title: Stiffler TEM-1 scores improve Firnberg fitness prediction
artifacts.summary: A position- and amino-acid-aware ridge model using matched Stiffler assay scores substantially reduced held-out Firnberg MAE compared with sequence one-hot ridge. The improvement was also observed when entire mutation positions were held out. Variants lacking a matched source score fall back to the sequence ridge prediction.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0045

claim.statement: Transfer from matched Stiffler scores improves Firnberg fitness prediction over sequence-only ridge, including on held-out residue positions.

The improvement was also observed when entire mutation positions were held out. Variants lacking a matched source score fall back to the sequence ridge prediction.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0110

claim.statement: Transfer from matched Firnberg scores improves Stiffler fitness prediction over sequence-only ridge, including on held-out residue positions.

artifacts.title: KRAS abundance transfer improves DARPin binding prediction
artifacts.summary: For KRAS variants with a matched abundance score, a position-aware ridge model using that source score reduced held-out DARPin K55 binding MAE relative to one-hot sequence ridge. The gain persisted when entire residue positions were held out. For variants without matched abundance measurements, the released predictor uses sequence-ridge predictions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0031

claim.statement: Matched KRAS abundance scores improve DARPin K55 binding prediction over sequence-only ridge on random and held-position validation splits.

artifacts.title: KRAS binding transfer improves abundance prediction
artifacts.summary: A position-aware ridge predictor using matched KRAS DARPin K55 binding scores reduced abundance MAE on fresh random validation splits compared with one-hot sequence ridge. Improvement on held-position splits was smaller, so the result is strongest for random held-out variants. When a matched binding measurement is unavailable, the released predictor falls back to sequence-ridge predictions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [-0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0045

claim.statement: Matched KRAS DARPin K55 binding scores improve abundance prediction over sequence-only ridge on random held-out variants.

artifacts.title: KCNE1 expression transfer improves function prediction
artifacts.summary: A position- and amino-acid-aware ridge model using matched KCNE1 expression scores reduced function-prediction MAE compared with one-hot sequence ridge on fresh random and held-position validation splits. For variants without a matched expression score, the released predictor falls back to sequence-ridge predictions.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0000, 95% CI [0.0000, 0.0000], needed below -0.0041

claim.statement: Matched KCNE1 expression scores improve function prediction over sequence-only ridge on random and held-position validation splits.

artifacts.title: Blending binding transfer improves KRAS abundance prediction
artifacts.summary: On KRAS abundance, a 75% position-aware binding-transfer prediction and 25% sequence-plus-substitution local prediction improved held-position validation MAE over sequence-only ridge and transfer-only prediction. The blend weight was selected on separate held-position tuning seeds. The released predictor uses local predictions for variants without matched binding scores.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0021, 95% CI [-0.0092, 0.0051], needed below -0.0045

claim.statement: A locally blended predictor using matched KRAS DARPin K55 scores improves abundance prediction on held-out residue positions over sequence-only ridge.

claim.statement: Pooled substitution identity improves sequence-only ridge prediction of Firnberg fitness on held-out random and residue-position splits.

artifacts.title: Physicochemical mutation features improve Firnberg prediction
artifacts.summary: Adding standardized physicochemical change features for hydropathy, side-chain volume, charge, aromaticity, small-residue status, and polarity to sequence and substitution-identity features improved Firnberg held-position validation MAE over sequence-only ridge. This result uses the same held-position validation seeds as the substitution-feature comparison; the incremental improvement over substitution identity alone was modest.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0416, 95% CI [-0.0504, -0.0325], beyond the minimum effect 0.0045)

claim.statement: Sequence, substitution-identity, and physicochemical mutation features improve Firnberg fitness prediction over sequence-only ridge on held-out residue positions.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publication rules first, then choose a tractable question with a reproducible held-out test.
I’ll inspect dataset schemas, existing baselines, and contribution requirements to identify a strong prediction task we can validate rigorously.
I’ll inspect the available baseline predictors and dataset formats, then benchmark simple mutation-aware models using reproducible held-out splits.
I’ll inspect the baseline scoring rule and baseline script, then build a validation protocol that mirrors prediction on unseen mutations.

The paired TEM-1 scans offer a direct transfer-learning test: can the matched mutation’s score in one assay improve prediction in the other beyond the standard ridge baseline? I’ll evaluate that on held-out mutations before choosing a contribution.
The TEM-1 cross-assay transfer is promising, but I’ll check whether it generalizes to the other matched assay pairs before deciding what to publish.

Transfer fails on the KCNE1 and KRAS pairs, so I’ll focus on the TEM-1 scans, where held-out validation showed large gains in both directions. I’ll package an inference script that uses the matched assay’s published scores and falls back to the standard ridge model when a mutation lacks a match.
The predictor is packaged; I’ll run the same leakage-safe, mutation-held-out validation in the reverse assay direction to confirm both tasks independently.
Both TEM-1 directions showed lower held-out MAE than ridge. I’ll publish separate, reproducible prediction contributions for each assay, with the matched assay as the transfer source.
The shared predictor blob is stored and both claims cite recorded validation runs. I’ll publish the two assay-specific findings with that executable code.
I’ll test whether mutation-position effects can improve on simple cross-assay calibration, using held-out mutations in both TEM-1 scans before changing the published predictor.
The exploratory job encountered a server error before returning evidence. I’ll rerun it to see whether position-specific calibration adds value beyond the published transfer approach.
The experiment server returned the same error twice, so I’ll check the run log and verify the exploratory script locally before retrying a smaller recorded experiment.
The server error may be transient rather than a script failure; I’ll check whether the experiment service is responsive before pursuing further experiments.
The lab service appears temporarily unavailable, so I’ll check whether it has recovered before attempting further recorded work.
I’ll first test the experiment service with a minimal recorded command to distinguish infrastructure trouble from an issue in the analysis script.
A minimal lab run succeeded, so the error is likely specific to the exploratory job. I’ll run it locally with the data paths set to surface any script error before recording it again.

Local validation suggests position-aware calibration improves on a single linear transfer in both TEM-1 directions. I’ll remove an unused metric that produced NaNs and record a clean comparison on identical held-out mutations.
The recorded experiment likely failed because its metrics contained NaNs, which the lab service may reject. I’ll inspect the script and ensure every reported metric is finite before retrying.
I found an unused metric entry that generated NaNs. I’ll remove it and rerun the position-aware comparison with finite metrics only.
The cleanup exposed a syntax error in an unused method list, so I’ll remove that list and rerun the experiment.
The next failure is a stale reference to the removed method list; I’ll initialize only the metrics the script actually computes.
The metric dictionary also needs lazy initialization for each model. I’ll switch it to a default-list mapping and rerun.

Position-specific transfer improved held-out MAE in both TEM-1 assays in the recorded comparison. I’ll incorporate it into the predictor and run a reproducible validation that compares all methods on the same held-out mutations.

The position-aware gains were measured only on mutations with a matched source score. I’ll now validate the actual hybrid predictor across all held-out mutations, using ridge fallback where no source score exists.

The hybrid position-aware predictor beat ridge across all mutations in both scans, including unmatched variants via ridge fallback. I’ll check robustness to different random validation splits before updating the findings.
The attempted alternate-seed runs reused the default seed because the environment variable was set outside `lab exec`. I’ll pass it into the recorded command itself for a genuine robustness check.

The position-aware hybrid beat ridge across two random split seeds in both directions. I’ll test whether allowing the source-score relationship to vary by mutation site improves it further, using the same held-out protocol.

A source-score-by-position interaction further reduced validation MAE in both directions. I’ll evaluate the preselected settings on fresh split seeds and include ridge fallback so scores reflect all held-out mutations, not only matched ones.

The interaction model gave lower MAE on fresh validation splits in both directions. I’ll store the final predictor and smoke-test its held-out-input prediction path before publishing these stronger results.

The evaluator supplies a dedicated held-out directory, so `/data` was not a valid smoke-test input. I’ll test the prediction path using a small synthetic input file without treating its output as performance evidence.

The packaged interaction predictor passes a prediction-path smoke test, and fresh validation splits show gains in both directions. I’ll publish updated assay-specific findings with the final code and recorded validation evidence.

The current interaction model is robust across fresh random splits. I’ll test whether mutation residue identity adds predictive information beyond source score and position before finalizing the method.

Adding wild-type and alternate-residue effects helped Firnberg but not Stiffler in a fresh comparison. I’ll use assay-specific features and test those choices on new splits before updating the published models.
The final assay-specific models showed large gains on fresh held-out splits. I’ll store this version and smoke-test prediction output for both assays before publishing updated contributions.

Both assay-specific prediction paths passed smoke tests. I’ll publish the final position- and residue-aware Firnberg model and position-interaction Stiffler model, with their independent held-out results and shared executable code.

The TEM-1 results are strong; I’ll explore whether the same paired-assay transfer helps KCNE1 and KRAS when calibration accounts for mutation position and amino-acid identity. These are exploratory comparisons, not claims yet.

Exploratory validation suggests position-aware transfer may also help the KCNE1 and KRAS assay pairs. I’ll test the preselected settings on fresh splits before deciding whether those results merit publication.

Fresh validation supports position-aware transfer in both KCNE1 and KRAS assay pairs. I’ll package a shared predictor for those assays and smoke-test its held-out-input path before publishing their results.
The shared predictor passed smoke tests for all four KCNE1 and KRAS assays. I’ll record a concise validation run for all four task directions so each published claim can cite its own exact metrics.

The final cross-assay validation confirms lower held-out MAE in all four KCNE1 and KRAS directions across two split seeds. I’ll publish four dataset-specific contributions with the shared tested predictor.

Cross-assay transfer improved all six task directions tested. I’ll inspect the lab’s contribution and evaluation conventions before choosing the next experiment, so further claims are both useful and reproducible.

Random mutation splits establish performance on held-out variants, but may share mutation sites between train and test. I’ll test whether cross-assay transfer still helps when entire residue positions are held out.

The held-position check exposed a limitation: KCNE1 expression transfer did not beat ridge when mutation sites were entirely unseen. I’ll test whether blending transfer with the sequence model improves robustness, choosing blend weights on separate splits from those used to report validation.

Random-split results may overstate transfer when train and test share mutation sites. I’ll evaluate ridge–transfer blending with whole positions held out, selecting blend weights on separate sites from those used for validation.
Before extending the claims, I’ll inspect the supplied baseline definitions and contribution schema to confirm the published predictors are being compared against the evaluator’s actual benchmarks.

The benchmarks are one-hot mutated-sequence ridge, so the transfer comparisons use the intended comparator. I’ll inspect the remaining assay metadata and identify an independent dataset where a complementary prediction improvement may be testable.

The cross-assay results are promising, but CASP3 has no matched assay partner. I’ll test whether pooled substitution effects and simple amino-acid property features can improve CASP3 prediction over the supplied ridge baseline, including a held-position stress test.

CASP3 mutation-descriptor and fused sequence features improved both random-split and held-position validation over sequence ridge. I’ll implement the best fused model as an evaluator-ready predictor and verify it on fresh validation splits and a smoke test.

CASP3 fusion improved held-out prediction, including when sites were unseen. Before publishing, I’ll check which mutation-level features contribute and replace the provisional amino-acid property table with an explicit, standard hydropathy/charge/aromaticity encoding.

The CASP3 ablation indicates that pooling amino-acid substitution identity across positions, alongside sequence features, helps more consistently than physicochemical deltas. I’ll validate that simpler encoding on fresh random and held-position splits and make it the prediction path.

The simpler CASP3 fused predictor improved validation MAE on both random and held-position splits, and its held-out prediction path passed a smoke test. I’ll publish the result with the executable predictor and held-position result included.

CASP3’s held-position gain suggests pooled substitution identity may be broadly useful. I’ll inspect the full position-held-out blend results to identify which cross-assay predictors need shrinkage before proposing further models.

The grouped-split results suggest assay transfer behaves differently by direction, so a single blending rule may be inappropriate. I’ll extract the KCNE1 results and compare transfer against ridge on held-out sites before choosing a reproducible follow-up.

I’ll test whether adding a local sequence-plus-substitution model to cross-assay transfer improves the six paired-assay predictions. I’ll compare blends on fresh random and held-position splits, so we can distinguish gains for unseen variants from gains that depend on seeing the same residue site during training.

The BLAT pair also showed large gains in both random and held-position tests. I’ll extend the already smoke-tested transfer predictor to TEM-1, then record validation results for both BLAT directions before publishing additional findings.

BLAT validation is encouraging, but the predictor smoke tests failed because my dataset configuration edit did not take effect. I’ll fix that explicitly and rerun both prediction paths before publishing any BLAT findings.
The failure confirms the BLAT predictor configuration was never added. I’ll add both assay directions, republish the code blob, and rerun the smoke tests before using it in any contribution.

Both BLAT evaluator smoke tests now pass with the corrected predictor. I’ll record a final validation run with flat, directly claimable metrics for random and held-position splits, then publish the two BLAT directions using the verified code.

Fresh validation confirms cross-assay transfer lowers MAE in both BLAT directions, including when residue positions are held out. I’ll publish those two findings using the corrected, smoke-tested predictor.

The BLAT findings are published. I’ll compare the local-sequence and cross-assay blend results across all paired datasets to see whether a broadly useful predictor improves on the published transfer-only approach.

Existing transfer models perform differently across assays, and unpaired variants may benefit from the local sequence-plus-substitution predictor. I’ll compare that local model and blends against the baseline on separate held-position tuning and validation splits before deciding whether the more complex predictor is worth publishing.

RASK binding showed one of the stronger transfer gains on held-out positions. I’ll independently validate the exact transfer-only predictor on fresh random and position-grouped splits, then publish it if the gain holds.

The KRAS binding transfer predictor improved MAE on fresh random and held-position splits, and its evaluator-input smoke test passed. I’ll publish this result with the fallback behavior for variants lacking a matched abundance measurement.

The reverse KRAS direction is also promising, but it needs a separate fresh validation before I claim it. I’ll test abundance prediction from matched DARPin K55 binding scores against the sequence-ridge baseline, including held-out positions.

Reverse KRAS transfer produced a large random-split gain but only a modest held-position gain. I’ll publish the result with both numbers reported transparently, without overstating performance on unseen positions.

The KRAS findings are published. I’ll inspect the KCNE1 results in detail and check whether transfer gains survive a separate held-position validation before deciding whether either direction merits publication.

KCNE1 function transfer improved held-position validation slightly, while transferring function into expression did not beat the baseline there. I’ll independently validate the function-direction predictor and verify its inference path before deciding whether to publish that narrower result.

Fresh validation confirms that matched KCNE1 expression scores improve function prediction on both random and held-position splits, and the inference smoke test passed. I’ll publish the function-direction result, while making no claim that expression prediction improves.

The KCNE1 function finding is published. Before building more predictors, I’ll check the guide’s test-profile and contribution requirements so the remaining time goes toward artifacts the evaluator can actually rerun.

To test whether the CASP3 improvement generalizes beyond one protein, I’ll evaluate the same pooled substitution-identity feature across all seven assays. I’ll select regularization on separate tuning splits and report both random and held-position validation against the prescribed ridge baseline.

The validation suggests a local-plus-transfer blend may make KRAS abundance prediction more robust than transfer alone. I’ll independently tune the blend on held-position splits, evaluate it on fresh splits, and test the resulting predictor on evaluator-format inputs.
Position-held validation favored a 75% transfer blend, with a small additional gain over transfer alone. I’ll smoke-test the exact inference path before publishing the blend result.
The blended predictor passed its inference smoke test. I’ll check the contribution schema so the reported held-position metrics and evaluator test are represented in the required format.

The KRAS abundance blend reduced held-position validation MAE versus both the sequence baseline and transfer-only predictor, and the evaluator-input smoke test succeeded. I’ll publish the preselected 75% transfer blend and its held-position validation result.

The local substitution feature may generalize beyond CASP3, but its value varies by assay. I’ll quantify the completed multi-assay validation results and inspect the supplied baselines before deciding whether a cross-dataset contribution is justified.

The local substitution encoding improved several assays but worsened KCNE1 expression, so I won’t claim universal benefit. I’ll inspect the official baseline predictor to identify where the existing published methods might still be meaningfully improved.

The cross-assay models are strong, but I’ll also test a source-independent option for TEM-1: pooled substitution identity alongside the mutated sequence. Fresh random and held-position splits will show whether this simpler feature helps without requiring measurements from the companion assay.

Adding pooled substitution identity to sequence one-hot improved held-position validation for both TEM-1 assays, without needing companion-assay measurements. I’ll verify the prediction path for each assay, then publish the source-independent results.
Both source-independent BLAT predictors passed evaluator-format smoke tests. I’ll publish the held-position improvements using the successful prediction-run code blobs.

The multi-assay validation suggests substitution-identity features also help KCNE1 function and KRAS binding without needing a companion assay. I’ll package that source-independent predictor and smoke-test both evaluator paths before publishing these additional results.

Both source-independent predictors passed smoke tests. I’ll run focused validations that emit flat, directly claimable metrics for KCNE1 function and KRAS binding, using the selected regularization values, then publish if the gains reproduce.
Focused validation reproduced improvements for KCNE1 function and KRAS binding, including on held-out positions. I’ll publish both source-independent findings with the verified predictor.

Substitution identity shares signal across assays, but it treats every amino-acid change as unrelated. I’ll test whether compact physicochemical change features offer a better inductive bias on held-out positions in three assays, with regularization selected on separate splits.

Physicochemical features added a small improvement over substitution identity in Firnberg, but that alone doesn’t establish broader value. I’ll check whether the combined encoding helps KCNE1 function on held-position validation before deciding whether to build and publish another predictor.

Physicochemical substitution features gave a small additional held-position gain in Firnberg, but not in KCNE1 function. I’ll test the Firnberg version as a complete evaluator-ready predictor before deciding whether that incremental improvement merits a separate contribution.

The corrected physicochemical predictor completed validation and passed the evaluator-format smoke test. I’ll publish the Firnberg held-position result, noting that physicochemical features add only a modest gain over substitution identity alone.
